title: Disciplinary differences in undergraduate students’ engagement with generative artificial intelligence
extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students’ engagement with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) differs across academic disciplines in higher education. The authors focus on whether disciplinary characteristics—especially Biglan’s pure/applied and hard/soft distinctions—are associated with students’ AI knowledge, intentions to use AI, and use of AI for different kinds of academic tasks. The study is motivated by the rapid spread of tools such as ChatGPT in universities and the lack of evidence about how students from different disciplinary cultures engage with these tools.

The study used a survey-based approach informed by an initial focus group discussion and pilot testing. The final questionnaire, administered via Google Forms, included closed-ended, open-ended, and Likert-style questions about GenAI knowledge, usage intention, and task-specific uses. Open-ended responses about academic uses of GenAI were coded into cognitive tasks (for example research assistance, brainstorming, complex homework support, substantive writing/editing, and advanced coding) and routine tasks (for example fact-checking, grammar correction, paraphrasing, translation, and learning reinforcement). The authors then used chi-square analyses to examine relationships between disciplinary category and AI engagement.

Participants were 193 undergraduates from a university in Singapore, drawn from disciplines grouped as hard-pure (science), hard-applied (engineering), soft-pure (humanities/arts/social sciences), and soft-applied (business). The survey was conducted from December 2023 to February 2024, following a preliminary focus group with 10 students and pilot testing with 30 students. Most respondents reported knowing about AI, and a large majority were already using it for academic purposes.

The main conclusion is that applied disciplines, whether hard or soft, show consistently higher AI knowledge and stronger intention to use AI than pure disciplines. The pure/applied distinction was more important than the hard/soft distinction in explaining GenAI engagement. Use of AI for routine tasks was relatively similar across disciplines, while use for cognitive tasks varied more substantially, with applied fields showing greater engagement. The authors argue that GenAI integration in higher education should be tailored to disciplinary cultures and task demands so that AI supports student learning without undermining core disciplinary knowledge and cognitive skill development.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model used for generating human-like text and supporting a wide range of language-based tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the GenAI tool students reported using for academic tasks; the paper examined disciplinary differences in knowledge, usage intention, and use of ChatGPT for cognitive versus routine academic tasks.

findings.finding_summary: In a survey of 193 undergraduates, ChatGPT engagement for cognitive tasks varied significantly by disciplinary category (χ2=8.140, p=0.043), with Hard-Applied and Soft-Applied fields showing higher engagement than Soft-Pure and Hard-Pure fields. By contrast, routine-task engagement did not significantly differ across the four disciplinary categories (χ2=6.367, p=0.095).
findings.measure: Self-reported ChatGPT engagement for cognitive tasks and routine tasks by disciplinary category

findings.finding_summary: The pure/applied distinction was significantly associated with ChatGPT engagement for both cognitive and routine tasks in the sample of 193 undergraduates. Applied fields showed higher engagement for cognitive tasks (χ2=7.955, p=0.005) and routine tasks (χ2=4.571, p=0.033) than pure fields.
findings.measure: Self-reported ChatGPT engagement for cognitive and routine academic tasks by pure/applied field classification

findings.finding_summary: The soft/hard disciplinary distinction was not significantly associated with ChatGPT engagement for either routine or cognitive tasks among 193 undergraduates. Reported tests were χ2=0.103, p=0.748 for routine tasks and χ2=0.540, p=0.462 for cognitive tasks.
findings.measure: Self-reported ChatGPT engagement for cognitive and routine academic tasks by soft/hard field classification

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative artificial intelligence tools broadly, including text-generating conversational systems used for academic support.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed across disciplines to assess students’ self-reported AI knowledge, usage intention/current use, and engagement in routine versus cognitive academic tasks.

findings.finding_summary: Students reported high overall familiarity with GenAI, with 94.3% indicating knowledge of AI, but knowledge differed significantly by disciplinary category (χ2=9.363, p=0.025). Applied fields had higher AI knowledge than pure fields, and the pure/applied distinction was significant (χ2=8.743, p=0.003), whereas the soft/hard distinction was not (χ2=1.945, p=0.163).
findings.measure: Self-reported AI knowledge by disciplinary category, pure/applied field, and soft/hard field

findings.finding_summary: AI usage was high overall, with 79.27% of students already using AI, 6.74% intending to use it, and 13.99% reporting no intention to use it. Usage intention differed significantly by disciplinary category (χ2=21.680, p=0.001), by pure/applied field (χ2=7.978, p=0.019), and by soft/hard field (χ2=6.057, p=0.048), with applied fields showing higher current adoption and hard fields showing greater future intention among non-users.
findings.measure: Self-reported AI usage intention/current use by disciplinary category, pure/applied field, and soft/hard field

findings.finding_summary: Across the full sample, students more often reported using GenAI for cognitive tasks (79.3%) than for routine tasks (65.3%). The study concludes that routine-task engagement was relatively consistent across disciplines, while cognitive-task engagement showed clearer disciplinary disparities, especially favoring applied fields.
findings.measure: Self-reported use of GenAI for cognitive versus routine academic tasks

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical survey/correlational study using chi-square analyses of self-reported knowledge and use, not an experimental or quasi-experimental design. The methodology is clear, but causal inference and objective learning outcomes are limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant differences in adoption and task engagement across disciplines, but no standardized effect sizes or direct student learning gains. Impact is therefore meaningful but unclear in magnitude.
